claim: Double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) binding and cleavage by Cas9 is a hallmark of type II CRISPR-Cas bacterial adaptive immunity.
source: Double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) binding and cleavage by Cas9 is a hallmark of type II CRISPR-Cas bacterial adaptive immunity.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about Cas9 function in CRISPR-Cas systems.

claim: All known Cas9 enzymes are thought to recognize DNA exclusively as a natural substrate.
source: All known Cas9 enzymes are thought to recognize DNA exclusively as a natural substrate, providing protection against DNA phage and plasmids.
evidence: This represents the prevailing understanding in the field prior to this study.

claim: Cas9 enzymes from both subtypes II-A and II-C can recognize and cleave single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) by an RNA-guided mechanism.
source: Here, we show that Cas9 enzymes from both subtypes II-A and II-C can recognize and cleave single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) by an RNA-guided mechanism that is independent of a protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM) sequence in the target RNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro cleavage assays shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNA-guided RNA cleavage by Cas9 is independent of a protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM) sequence in the target RNA.
source: Here, we show that Cas9 enzymes from both subtypes II-A and II-C can recognize and cleave single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) by an RNA-guided mechanism that is independent of a protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM) sequence in the target RNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cleavage assays without PAMmer and with mutant PAM sequences shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: RNA-guided RNA cleavage by Cas9 is programmable and site-specific.
source: RNA-guided RNA cleavage is programmable and site-specific, and we find that this activity can be exploited to reduce infection by single-stranded RNA phage in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by the MS2 phage screen data in Figure 3 and cleavage mapping in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: Cas9 RNA-targeting activity can be exploited to reduce infection by single-stranded RNA phage in vivo.
source: RNA-guided RNA cleavage is programmable and site-specific, and we find that this activity can be exploited to reduce infection by single-stranded RNA phage in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MS2 phage protection experiments shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Cas9 can direct PAM-independent repression of gene expression in bacteria.
source: We also demonstrate that Cas9 can direct PAM-independent repression of gene expression in bacteria.
evidence: This is shown by the GFP repression experiments in Figure 4.

claim: A subset of Cas9 enzymes have the ability to act on both DNA and RNA target sequences.
source: These results indicate that a subset of Cas9 enzymes have the ability to act on both DNA and RNA target sequences, and suggest the potential for use in programmable RNA targeting applications.
evidence: This is inferred from the demonstration of RNA cleavage activity in Cas9 enzymes known to cleave DNA.

claim: Prokaryotic CRISPR-Cas systems provide immunity against plasmids and bacteriophage by using foreign DNA stored as CRISPR spacer sequences together with Cas nucleases to stop infection.
source: Prokaryotic clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR)-CRISPR-associated (Cas) systems provide immunity against plasmids and bacteriophage by using foreign DNA stored as CRISPR spacer sequences together with Cas nucleases to stop infection (Wright et al., 2016; Mohanraju et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cas9 employs a CRISPR RNA (crRNA) and a trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA) to target spacer-complementary regions (protospacers) on foreign genetic elements to guide double-stranded DNA cleavage.
source: One such nuclease, Cas9 of the type II systems, employs a CRISPR RNA (crRNA) and a trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA) to target spacer-complementary regions (protospacers) on the foreign genetic element to guide double-stranded DNA cleavage (Jinek et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) must be present for the Cas9-RNA complex to bind and cleave DNA.
source: A protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) must also be present for the Cas9-RNA complex to bind and cleave DNA (Jinek et al., 2012; Gasiunas et al., 2012; Anders et al., 2014; Szczelkun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Combining the crRNA and tracrRNA into a chimeric, single-guide RNA (sgRNA) simplified the system for widespread adoption as a versatile genome editing technology.
source: Combining the crRNA and tracrRNA into a chimeric, single-guide RNA (sgRNA) simplified the system for widespread adoption as a versatile genome editing technology (Jinek et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Both genetic and biochemical data support the conclusion that in vivo, Cas9 is exclusively a DNA-targeting enzyme.
source: To date, both genetic and biochemical data support the conclusion that in vivo, Cas9 is exclusively a DNA-targeting enzyme.
evidence: This represents the prevailing understanding prior to this study.

claim: S. pyogenes Cas9 (SpyCas9) can be supplied with a short DNA oligo containing the PAM sequence (a PAMmer) to induce single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) binding and cutting.
source: For example, the S. pyogenes Cas9 (SpyCas9) can be supplied with a short DNA oligo containing the PAM sequence (a PAMmer) to induce single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) binding and cutting (O'Connell et al., 2014; Nelles et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: SpyCas9 can be used to target repetitive RNAs and repress translation in certain mRNAs in the absence of a PAMmer.
source: More recently, it was demonstrated that SpyCas9 could be used to target repetitive RNAs and repress translation in certain mRNAs in the absence of a PAMmer (Liu et al., 2016; Batra et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Francisella novicida Cas9 (FnoCas9) has been implicated in degradation of a specific mRNA but through a mechanism independent of RNA-based cleavage.
source: A different Cas9 homolog from Francisella novicida (FnoCas9) has been implicated in degradation of a specific mRNA but through a mechanism independent of RNA-based cleavage (Sampson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Some Cas9 homologs can target single-stranded DNA substrates under some conditions.
source: Together with evidence that some Cas9 homologs can target single-stranded DNA substrates under some conditions (Ma et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015), these studies raised the possibility that certain Cas9 enzymes might have intrinsic RNA-guided RNA cleavage activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: S. aureus Cas9 (SauCas9) and C. jejuni Cas9 (CjeCas9) direct cleavage of RNA in the absence of a PAMmer when programmed with a cognate sgRNA.
source: When programmed with a cognate sgRNA, S. aureus Cas9 (SauCas9) and C. jejuni Cas9 (CjeCas9) direct cleavage of RNA in the absence of a PAMmer (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cleavage assays shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No RNA cleavage was detected using SpyCas9 without a PAMmer.
source: No RNA cleavage was detected using SpyCas9, which requires a PAMmer for efficient RNA cleavage in vitro (O'Connell et al., 2014), or using F. novicida Cas9 (FnoCas9).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C, and is consistent with prior work cited.

claim: No RNA cleavage was detected using F. novicida Cas9 (FnoCas9).
source: No RNA cleavage was detected using SpyCas9, which requires a PAMmer for efficient RNA cleavage in vitro (O'Connell et al., 2014), or using F. novicida Cas9 (FnoCas9).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The cleavage efficiencies for both SauCas9 and CjeCas9 are indistinguishable.
source: While the cleavage efficiencies for both SauCas9 and CjeCas9 are indistinguishable (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), we focused on the activity of SauCas9 due to the abundance of mechanistic and structural data for this enzyme (Nishimasu et al., 2015; Friedland et al., 2015; Ran et al., 2015; Kleinstiver et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: RNA targeting by SauCas9 requires the presence of a guide RNA.
source: RNA targeting by SauCas9 requires the presence of a guide RNA and a catalytically-active protein, as both apo protein lacking the guide RNA and a catalytically inactive mutant (D10A and N580A) do not cleave RNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the control experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: RNA targeting by SauCas9 requires a catalytically-active protein.
source: RNA targeting by SauCas9 requires the presence of a guide RNA and a catalytically-active protein, as both apo protein lacking the guide RNA and a catalytically inactive mutant (D10A and N580A) do not cleave RNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the control experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Addition of EDTA to chelate divalent metal ions abolished RNA cleavage by SauCas9.
source: Furthermore, addition of EDTA to chelate divalent metal ions abolished RNA cleavage, verifying that divalent metal ions are necessary for catalysis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Divalent metal ions are necessary for RNA cleavage catalysis by SauCas9.
source: Furthermore, addition of EDTA to chelate divalent metal ions abolished RNA cleavage, verifying that divalent metal ions are necessary for catalysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the EDTA inhibition experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: SauCas9 RNA cleavage is single-turnover.
source: As with DNA substrates (Sternberg et al., 2014), incubation of SauCas9 with an excess of RNA target demonstrated that cleavage is single-turnover (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the excess substrate experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C and is consistent with prior work on DNA substrates.

claim: The predominant RNA cleavage site by SauCas9 is shifted by one nucleotide compared to the site of DNA cleavage.
source: Hydrolysis mapping of the cleavage product revealed that the predominant RNA cleavage site is shifted by one nucleotide compared to the site of DNA cleavage (Garneau et al., 2010; Jinek et al., 2012; Gasiunas et al., 2012) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is shown by the cleavage site mapping in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: The shift in RNA cleavage site is consistent with that observed for PAM-dependent SpyCas9 RNA-cleavage.
source: The shift is consistent with that observed for PAM-dependent SpyCas9 RNA-cleavage (O'Connell et al., 2014) and is likely due to the more compact geometry of an RNA-RNA helix relative to an RNA-DNA hybrid helix (Wang et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to prior work and structural considerations.

claim: The shift in RNA cleavage site is likely due to the more compact geometry of an RNA-RNA helix relative to an RNA-DNA hybrid helix.
source: The shift is consistent with that observed for PAM-dependent SpyCas9 RNA-cleavage (O'Connell et al., 2014) and is likely due to the more compact geometry of an RNA-RNA helix relative to an RNA-DNA hybrid helix (Wang et al., 1982).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on structural knowledge.

claim: SauCas9 targets ssRNA in the absence of a PAMmer.
source: SauCas9 targets ssRNA in the absence of a PAMmer, a contrast to SpyCas9 targeting of ssRNA (O'Connell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cleavage assays in Figure 1 and contrasted with SpyCas9 behavior.

claim: SauCas9 in vitro ssRNA cleavage in the presence of a PAMmer is two-fold slower than the reaction with only target ssRNA.
source: Testing SauCas9 in vitro ssRNA cleavage in the presence of a PAMmer (30x molar excess over ssRNA target) revealed that turn-over was two-fold slower than the reaction with only target ssRNA (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is shown by the kinetic data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The complementary PAMmer impairs RNA cleavage activity by SauCas9.
source: SauCas9 ssRNA cleavage conducted in the presence of a non-complementary, control DNA oligo did not yield a similar reduction in cleavage rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), indicating that the complementary PAMmer impairs RNA cleavage activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of PAMmer and control oligo effects shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Single-stranded RNA that is not complementary to the sgRNA is not cleaved by SauCas9.
source: Consistent with cleavage being guide-dependent, single-stranded RNA that is not complementary to the sgRNA is not cleaved (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by the specificity controls in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) is not a substrate for SauCas9.
source: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) is also not a substrate for SauCas9.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Increasing the length of the targeting region of the guide up to 23 nt results in tighter binding and more efficient cleavage by SauCas9.
source: Increasing the length of the targeting region of the guide up to 23 nt results in tighter binding and more efficient cleavage (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), mirroring the preference for longer guides for DNA cleavage (Ran et al., 2015; Friedland et al., 2015).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the guide length experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Extending the guide strand complementarity to the target beyond 23 nt did not increase RNA target binding or cleavage efficiency.
source: Extending the guide strand complementarity to the target beyond 23 nt did not increase RNA target binding or cleavage efficiency, indicating that 23 nt is the optimal length for in vitro binding and targeting applications.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: 23 nt is the optimal length for in vitro binding and targeting applications with SauCas9.
source: Extending the guide strand complementarity to the target beyond 23 nt did not increase RNA target binding or cleavage efficiency, indicating that 23 nt is the optimal length for in vitro binding and targeting applications.
evidence: This is inferred from the guide length optimization data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The apparent dissociation constant (Kd,app) of the SauCas9-sgRNA complex (23 nt targeting region) for the ssRNA target is 1.8 ± 0.09 nM.
source: The apparent dissociation constant (Kd,app) of the SauCas9-sgRNA complex (23 nt targeting region) for the ssRNA target is 1.8 ± 0.09 nM (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D), which is ~5 x weaker than the 0.34 ± 0.03 nM binding affinity measured for a dsDNA substrate of the same sequence.
evidence: This is measured by filter binding assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: The binding affinity of SauCas9-sgRNA for ssRNA is ~5 x weaker than for a dsDNA substrate of the same sequence.
source: The apparent dissociation constant (Kd,app) of the SauCas9-sgRNA complex (23 nt targeting region) for the ssRNA target is 1.8 ± 0.09 nM (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D), which is ~5 x weaker than the 0.34 ± 0.03 nM binding affinity measured for a dsDNA substrate of the same sequence.
evidence: This is calculated from the binding data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: SauCas9-catalyzed ssRNA cleavage is limited to ~30% fraction cleaved.
source: We noted that SauCas9-catalyzed ssRNA cleavage is limited to ~30% fraction cleaved (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), compared to >80% fraction cleaved for ssDNA and dsDNA targets.
evidence: This is observed in the cleavage assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: SauCas9 cleavage of ssDNA and dsDNA targets reaches >80% fraction cleaved.
source: We noted that SauCas9-catalyzed ssRNA cleavage is limited to ~30% fraction cleaved (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), compared to >80% fraction cleaved for ssDNA and dsDNA targets.
evidence: This is observed in the cleavage assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Greater thermodynamic stability of RNA secondary structures, relative to those in ssDNA, might occlude SauCas9-sgRNA binding to an ssRNA target sequence.
source: Greater thermodynamic stability of RNA secondary structures, relative to those in ssDNA (Bercy and Bockelmann, 2015), might occlude SauCas9-sgRNA binding to an ssRNA target sequence, a possibility that we tested using a panel of partially duplexed RNA substrates (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by the structured RNA experiments in Figure 2.

claim: Introduction of a short segment of mismatched base pairs to mimic partially unwound dsDNA substrates enhances the ability of type II-C Cas9s to unwind and cleave dsDNA.
source: Previously, introduction of a short segment of mismatched base pairs to mimic partially unwound dsDNA substrates was shown to enhance the ability of type II-C Cas9s (including CjeCas9) to unwind and cleave dsDNA (Ma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Duplex-RNA substrates containing a 2- or 6-base pair mismatched segment located near the 5' or 3' end of the 23 nt guide RNA region could not be cleaved by SauCas9.
source: Here, we found that duplex-RNA substrates containing a 2- or 6-base pair mismatched segment located near the 5' or 3' end of the 23 nt guide RNA region of the sgRNA could not be cleaved (Figure 2A–C, substrates 5, 6, 10, and 11).
evidence: This is shown by the structured RNA cleavage assays in Figure 2A–C.

claim: When the unpaired region in duplex-RNA substrates was increased to 12-base pairs, SauCas9 was able to cleave the target strand.
source: However, when the unpaired region was increased to 12-base pairs, SauCas9 was able to cleave the target strand.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A–C, substrates 7 and 12.

claim: There is a slight cleavage preference for RNA substrates in which the 12-base pair mismatched segment is located near the 5´ end of the guide sequence of the sgRNA.
source: There was a slight cleavage preference for RNA substrates in which the 12-base pair mismatched segment is located near the 5´ end of the guide sequence of the sgRNA (Figure 2A–C, substrates 7 and 12).
evidence: This is observed in the cleavage data in Figure 2A–C.

claim: The 23-base pair mismatched segment RNA substrates ('Bubble' substrates 8 and 9) are targeted more efficiently than their ssRNA counterparts (substrates 1 and 2).
source: Interestingly, the 23-base pair mismatched segment RNA substrates ('Bubble' substrates 8 and 9) are targeted more efficiently than their ssRNA counterparts (substrates 1 and 2) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown by the cleavage efficiency data in Figure 2C.

claim: Both the 23-base pair mismatched segment RNA and ssRNA substrates are bound with similar affinity by SauCas9.
source: We measured the binding affinity of all substrates and found that both the 23-base pair mismatched segment RNA and ssRNA substrates are bound with similar affinity (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown by the binding data in Figure 2D.

claim: The apparent difference in cleavage efficiency between bubble and ssRNA substrates is not due to the presence of a double-stranded PAM sequence.
source: Furthermore, the apparent difference in cleavage efficiency was not due to the presence of a double-stranded PAM sequence, as mutating the PAM region does not impair cleavage (Figure 2C, compare substrates 8 and 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PAM mutant controls in Figure 2C.

claim: RNA containing a mismatched segment presents a more accessible substrate to the Cas9-sgRNA complex due to stable annealing between the ends of the non-target and target strands.
source: We hypothesize that RNA containing a mismatched segment presents a more accessible substrate to the Cas9-sgRNA complex due to stable annealing between the ends of the non-target and target strands, whereas the ssRNA substrate alone has ends that are predicted to stabilize a conformation that is partially structured and therefore inaccessible (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural predictions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ssRNA substrate alone has ends that are predicted to stabilize a conformation that is partially structured and therefore inaccessible.
source: We hypothesize that RNA containing a mismatched segment presents a more accessible substrate to the Cas9-sgRNA complex due to stable annealing between the ends of the non-target and target strands, whereas the ssRNA substrate alone has ends that are predicted to stabilize a conformation that is partially structured and therefore inaccessible (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on structural predictions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Spiking reactions with fresh SauCas9 protein alone or SauCas9 RNP after reactions reached equilibrium did not increase the amount of ssRNA cleavage.
source: To test this, we spiked reactions with fresh SauCas9 protein alone or SauCas9 RNP after reactions reached equilibrium; however, we did not observe an increase in the amount of ssRNA cleavage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is shown by the spike-in experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Addition of a second target ssRNA complementary to the guide RNA resulted in a burst of cleavage activity.
source: After 1 hr of incubation, the addition of a second target ssRNA complementary to the guide RNA resulted in a burst of cleavage activity, whereas a non-complementary ssRNA substrate did not stimulate cleavage.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: The second target ssRNA is cleaved to a comparable extent to that observed when this second target was the only substrate in the reaction.
source: The second target ssRNA is cleaved to a comparable extent to that observed when this second target was the only substrate in the reaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E, compare reactions 1 and 3).
evidence: This is shown by the sequential cleavage data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: SauCas9 RNP is still competent and available for cleavage at the end of the reaction.
source: These observations suggest that SauCas9 RNP is still competent and available for cleavage at the end of the reaction and that a property intrinsic to the ssRNA substrate is the limiting factor.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequential cleavage experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: A property intrinsic to the ssRNA substrate is the limiting factor for cleavage extent.
source: These observations suggest that SauCas9 RNP is still competent and available for cleavage at the end of the reaction and that a property intrinsic to the ssRNA substrate is the limiting factor.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequential cleavage and spike-in experiments.

claim: The observed difference in cleavage extents for various RNA substrates reflects the fraction of molecules that are structurally accessible for cleavage by the SauCas9 RNP.
source: We propose that the observed difference in cleavage extents for various RNA substrates reflects the fraction of molecules that are structurally accessible for cleavage by the SauCas9 RNP.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on the structured RNA experiments.

claim: A plasmid library encoding sgRNAs containing guide sequences complementary to the genome of MS2 was generated.
source: To test this, we generated a plasmid library encoding sgRNAs containing guide sequences complementary to the genome of MS2, a single-stranded RNA phage that can infect E. coli.
evidence: This is described in the methods and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A subset of sgRNAs in the library contained scrambled guide sequences that should not target MS2, providing negative controls.
source: A subset of these sgRNAs contained scrambled guide sequences that should not target MS2, providing negative controls.
evidence: This is part of the experimental design described in the text.

claim: Another sgRNA subset included single-nucleotide mismatches introduced at each position of a target sequence to test for mismatch sensitivity in ssRNA recognition.
source: Another sgRNA subset included single-nucleotide mismatches introduced at each position of a target sequence to test for mismatch sensitivity in ssRNA recognition.
evidence: This is part of the experimental design described in the text.

claim: The plasmid library comprised 18,114 sgRNAs.
source: This plasmid library, comprising 18,114 sgRNAs, was co-transformed into E. coli along with a vector encoding a catalytically active version of SauCas9 and the population of transformants was subjected to infection by bacteriophage MS2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the description of the experimental design.

claim: Between 131 and 166 sgRNAs were significantly enriched (FDR-adjusted p-value<0.05) in the two different MS2 infection conditions.
source: We identified between 131 and 166 sgRNAs that were significantly enriched (false discovery rate (FDR)-adjusted p-value<0.05) in the two different MS2 infection conditions (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is the result of the MS2 screen analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The majority of enriched sgRNAs were perfectly complementary to the MS2 genome.
source: The majority of these sgRNAs were perfectly complementary to the MS2 genome, and only three and five control sgRNAs (out of 708 total control sgRNAs) for the MOI-10 and −100 conditions, respectively, were enriched (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in the screen results in Figure 3B.

claim: Only three and five control sgRNAs (out of 708 total control sgRNAs) for the MOI-10 and −100 conditions, respectively, were enriched.
source: The majority of these sgRNAs were perfectly complementary to the MS2 genome, and only three and five control sgRNAs (out of 708 total control sgRNAs) for the MOI-10 and −100 conditions, respectively, were enriched (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in the screen results in Figure 3B.

claim: The lengths of enriched guide sequences were skewed toward shorter targeting lengths.
source: The lengths of enriched guide sequences were skewed toward shorter targeting lengths (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, left); however, this likely reflects bias in the cloned input library since the ratio between the enriched guide sequences and those of the library without phage selection are similar (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The skew toward shorter guide lengths likely reflects bias in the cloned input library.
source: The lengths of enriched guide sequences were skewed toward shorter targeting lengths (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, left); however, this likely reflects bias in the cloned input library since the ratio between the enriched guide sequences and those of the library without phage selection are similar (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, right).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of enriched guides to the input library shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The 23-nt guide segment sgRNAs were preferentially enriched over those of shorter length.
source: When comparing the degree of enrichment between the different guide lengths, the 23-nt guide segment sgRNAs were preferentially enriched over those of shorter length (Figure 3C), consistent with the in vitro observation that longer guides are more efficient for directing ssRNA cleavage (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and is consistent with in vitro data.

claim: There was no specific sequence bias in the enriched guides relative to those in the unselected library.
source: To assess whether there was any sequence bias within the enriched guides, we aligned guide sequences of all lengths at their 3' end. These alignments showed no specific sequence bias in the enriched guides relative to those in the unselected library (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by the sequence logo analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The absence of sequence bias is consistent with the crystal structure of an SauCas9-sgRNA-DNA-bound complex which revealed the absence of base-specific contacts of Cas9 to the target strand.
source: This is consistent with the crystal structure of an SauCas9-sgRNA-DNA-bound complex which revealed the absence of base-specific contacts of Cas9 to the target strand (Nishimasu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural data.

claim: Enriched guide sequences were clustered at specific regions of the MS2 genome.
source: Strikingly, mapping enriched guide sequences onto the MS2 genome showed that enriched sgRNAs were clustered at specific regions, which were consistent across both experimental conditions (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown by the genome mapping in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The targeting 'hotspots' are regions of low structural complexity.
source: Together with our biochemical data suggesting that SauCas9 cannot bind or cleave structured RNAs (Figure 3), we interpret these targeting 'hotspots' to be regions of low structural complexity.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of biochemical data and the MS2 screen results.

claim: sgRNAs containing different guide segment lengths overlap at hotspot regions.
source: It is important to note that sgRNAs containing different guide segment lengths overlap at these regions, possibly indicating that increases in targeting efficiency due to guide length are secondary to target accessibility to the Cas9 RNP.
evidence: This is observed in the genome mapping data in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Increases in targeting efficiency due to guide length are secondary to target accessibility to the Cas9 RNP.
source: It is important to note that sgRNAs containing different guide segment lengths overlap at these regions, possibly indicating that increases in targeting efficiency due to guide length are secondary to target accessibility to the Cas9 RNP.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the overlapping hotspots.

claim: Guides targeted not only single-stranded, accessible regions but also those that form apparently stable secondary structures in the MS2 genome structure.
source: Guides targeted not only single-stranded, accessible regions but also those that form apparently stable secondary structures.
evidence: This is observed when mapping guides to the MS2 structure shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The structure of the MS2 genome was determined on the intact phage particle and may not represent the RNA structure(s) relevant to the infection stage during which SauCas9-mediated protection is crucial.
source: The structure of the MS2 genome was determined on the intact phage particle, however, and may not represent the RNA structure(s) relevant to the infection stage during which SauCas9-mediated protection is crucial.
evidence: This is a caveat noted about the structural interpretation.

claim: Reconstitution of SauCas9 with a targeting guide confers approximately a ten-fold protection against the RNA phage MS2.
source: Reconstitution of SauCas9 with a targeting guide confers approximately a ten-fold protection against the RNA phage (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is shown by the plaque assay data in Figure 3E,F.

claim: No protection against MS2 was observed in the absence of an sgRNA or SauCas9 protein.
source: No protection was observed in the absence of an sgRNA or SauCas9 protein.
evidence: This is shown by the controls in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Scrambling the sequence of the guide abrogates protection against MS2.
source: Scrambling the sequence of the guide also abrogates protection, confirming that sequence complementary is necessary for phage elimination.
evidence: This is shown by the scrambled guide controls in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Sequence complementarity is necessary for phage elimination.
source: Scrambling the sequence of the guide also abrogates protection, confirming that sequence complementary is necessary for phage elimination.
evidence: This is inferred from the scrambled guide control experiments.

claim: Guide segments of all lengths tested (20–23 nts) conferred protection to a similar level.
source: Guide segments of all lengths tested (20–23 nts) conferred protection to a similar level (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B), consistent with the result from the MS2 screen that guide segments of all lengths were enriched in 'hotspot' regions (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Two 'control' guides were enriched in both the MOI-10 and −100 treatments and conferred protection.
source: Two 'control' guides were enriched in both the MOI-10 and −100 treatments. Interestingly, both guides conferred protection but their scrambled counterparts did not (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: A possible off-target binding site was found for guide #14238 within the MS2 genome.
source: Whereas a possible off-target binding site was found for one guide (#14238) within the MS2 genome (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E), it remains unclear how guide #14210 confers protection.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E.

claim: It remains unclear how guide #14210 confers protection.
source: Whereas a possible off-target binding site was found for one guide (#14238) within the MS2 genome (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E), it remains unclear how guide #14210 confers protection.
evidence: This is stated as an unresolved question.

claim: Guide #14210 possibly acts by targeting an E. coli host factor that is necessary for infection.
source: Possibly this sgRNA acts by targeting an E. coli host factor that is necessary for infection.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed protection.

claim: On average, short guides were less sensitive to mismatches in the MS2 screen.
source: We observed a pronounced gradient of increasing guide stringency with length. On average, short guides were less sensitive to mismatches, while mismatches in longer sgRNAs led to decreased recovery compared to control samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: This is shown by the mismatch analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A,B.

claim: Mismatches in longer sgRNAs led to decreased recovery compared to control samples in the MS2 screen.
source: We observed a pronounced gradient of increasing guide stringency with length. On average, short guides were less sensitive to mismatches, while mismatches in longer sgRNAs led to decreased recovery compared to control samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: This is shown by the mismatch analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A,B.

claim: There is a correlation between mismatches in the MS2 screen and in vitro biochemical cleavage assays for the sgRNA with a 23 nt guide segment sequence.
source: Nevertheless, despite potential noise introduced in this analysis due to guide segments that target inaccessible MS2 regions, we observe an interesting correlation between mismatches in the MS2 screen and in vitro biochemical cleavage assays for the sgRNA with a 23 nt guide segment sequence (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C,D).
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figure 3—figure supplement 4A,B with 4C,D.

claim: The first few nucleotides in the 'seed' region (guide 3´ end proximal) are sensitive to mismatches.
source: The first few nucleotides in the 'seed' region (guide 3´ end proximal) are sensitive to mismatches, while a central region of sensitivity is also observed, similar to previously demonstrated regions of sensitivity for SpyCas9 DNA cleavage (Cong et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2016; Gorski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and is consistent with prior work.

claim: A central region of sensitivity to mismatches is observed, similar to previously demonstrated regions of sensitivity for SpyCas9 DNA cleavage.
source: The first few nucleotides in the 'seed' region (guide 3´ end proximal) are sensitive to mismatches, while a central region of sensitivity is also observed, similar to previously demonstrated regions of sensitivity for SpyCas9 DNA cleavage (Cong et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2016; Gorski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and is consistent with prior work.

claim: When using sgRNAs designed to recognize a sequence in the GFP gene adjacent to the appropriate PAM for SauCas9 or SpyCas9, GFP expression is significantly reduced.
source: When using sgRNAs designed to recognize a sequence in the GFP gene adjacent to the appropriate PAM for SauCas9 (NNGRRT) or SpyCas9 (NGG), GFP expression is significantly reduced (Figure 4A) consistent with CRISPR-interference (CRISPRi) (Qi et al., 2013; Gilbert et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and is consistent with prior CRISPRi work.

claim: When sgRNAs were designed to recognize GFP sequences not flanked by a PAM, dSauCas9 but not dSpyCas9 was able to repress GFP expression.
source: When sgRNAs were designed to recognize GFP sequences not flanked by a PAM, dSauCas9 but not dSpyCas9 was able to repress GFP expression.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SauCas9-mediated GFP repression was dependent on sgRNAs that target the coding strand.
source: The SauCas9-mediated GFP repression was dependent on sgRNAs that target the coding strand; sgRNAs that recognize the non-coding strand did not result in reduced GFP expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The length of the targeting sequence in vivo corroborates in vitro data, with longer guides working more efficiently.
source: The length of the targeting sequence in vivo corroborates in vitro data, with longer guides working more efficiently (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and is consistent with in vitro data.

claim: Different guide sequences display variable efficiencies of targeting in GFP repression.
source: Different guide sequences display variable efficiencies of targeting. We tiled sgRNAs across the GFP mRNA sequence to test the robustness of dSauCas9 to repress GFP expression (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown by the tiling experiment in Figure 4C.

claim: Some dSauCas9 RNPs reduced GFP signal to 15–30% of that observed in the presence of the sgRNA alone.
source: The efficiency of dSauCas9-mediated GFP repression varied according to the target sequence, with some dSauCas9 RNPs reducing GFP signal to 15–30% of that observed in the presence of the sgRNA alone (Figure 4C, GFP2 and 6) and others showing no ability to repress GFP expression (GFP7 and 9).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Some dSauCas9 RNPs showed no ability to repress GFP expression.
source: The efficiency of dSauCas9-mediated GFP repression varied according to the target sequence, with some dSauCas9 RNPs reducing GFP signal to 15–30% of that observed in the presence of the sgRNA alone (Figure 4C, GFP2 and 6) and others showing no ability to repress GFP expression (GFP7 and 9).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Electrophoretic mobility shift assays support the conclusion that repression is not occurring at the dsDNA level by promiscuous PAM binding.
source: Electrophoretic mobility shift assays support the conclusion that repression is not occurring at the dsDNA level by promiscuous PAM binding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Repression is largely equivalent between catalytically active and inactive forms of SauCas9.
source: Repression is largely equivalent between catalytically active and inactive forms of SauCas9 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that binding of the Cas9-sgRNA complex to the mRNA is sufficient for repression and consistent with in vitro data showing that the enzyme does not catalyze multiple-turnover RNA cleavage.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Binding of the Cas9-sgRNA complex to the mRNA is sufficient for repression.
source: Repression is largely equivalent between catalytically active and inactive forms of SauCas9 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that binding of the Cas9-sgRNA complex to the mRNA is sufficient for repression and consistent with in vitro data showing that the enzyme does not catalyze multiple-turnover RNA cleavage.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of active and inactive Cas9 in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SauCas9 can readily bind and cleave bacteriophage RNA and mRNA sequences that are exposed and unstructured.
source: Together our biochemical and in vivo data support a model in which SauCas9 can readily bind and cleave bacteriophage RNA and mRNA sequences that are exposed and unstructured (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the combined data.

claim: Regions that form strong structures are inaccessible to SauCas9 RNP binding, thereby preventing cleavage or repression activity.
source: Regions that form strong structures are inaccessible to SauCas9 RNP binding, thereby preventing cleavage or repression activity.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the structured RNA data.

claim: RNA occluded by RNA-binding proteins would be recalcitrant to cleavage by Cas9.
source: As Cas9 cleavage activity is limited by target accessibility, we expect that RNA occluded by RNA-binding proteins would also be recalcitrant to cleavage.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the accessibility model.

claim: Type II-A and type II-C Cas9 enzymes can catalyze programmable and PAM-independent single-stranded RNA cleavage.
source: Here, we present evidence that type II-A and type II-C Cas9 enzymes can catalyze programmable and PAM-independent single-stranded RNA cleavage.
evidence: This is the main conclusion summarized in the Discussion.

claim: SauCas9 can be employed both biochemically and in cells to cleave RNA and regulate genes on both the transcriptional and translational level in parallel by accounting for target site PAM proximity.
source: Focusing on SauCas9, we show that this enzyme can be employed both biochemically and in cells to cleave RNA and regulate genes on both the transcriptional and translational level in parallel by accounting for target site PAM proximity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the combined in vitro and in vivo experiments.

claim: SauCas9 ssRNA scission requires only an sgRNA and does not need a PAMmer.
source: Importantly, SauCas9 ssRNA scission requires only an sgRNA and does not need a PAMmer, thereby simplifying applications (Nelles et al., 2015) and facilitating delivery to cells as a pre-assembled RNP (Zuris et al., 2015; Mout et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a key finding with practical implications.

claim: The RNA-targeting capability of SauCas9 and related Cas9 enzymes offers the advantage of repressing viruses whose lifecycles do not involve a DNA genome or intermediate.
source: The RNA-targeting capability of SauCas9 and related Cas9 enzymes offers the advantage of repressing viruses whose lifecycles do not involve a DNA genome or intermediate, thereby rendering them inaccessible to Cas9-mediated DNA cleavage.
evidence: This is a potential application discussed based on the MS2 results.

claim: SauCas9 could be programmed to confer protection to E. coli against MS2, an RNA bacteriophage with no DNA intermediate.
source: We demonstrated that SauCas9 could be programmed to confer protection to E. coli against MS2, an RNA bacteriophage with no DNA intermediate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MS2 protection experiments.

claim: Whether RNA-based viral repression by Cas9 occurs in natural systems is not known, but seems possible based on our results.
source: Whether RNA-based viral repression by Cas9 occurs in natural systems is not known, but seems possible based on our results.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about biological relevance.

claim: DNA cleavage by SauCas9 remains more rapid than RNA cleavage.
source: DNA cleavage by SauCas9 remains more rapid than RNA cleavage, indicating that DNA-targeting is probably the biologically preferred method for phage and plasmid interference.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data comparing DNA and RNA cleavage.

claim: DNA-targeting is probably the biologically preferred method for phage and plasmid interference.
source: DNA cleavage by SauCas9 remains more rapid than RNA cleavage, indicating that DNA-targeting is probably the biologically preferred method for phage and plasmid interference.
evidence: This is inferred from the relative kinetics of DNA vs RNA cleavage.

claim: Cas9 activity on RNA is PAM-independent and may mitigate the effects of PAM-escape mutants that would evade DNA-level interference.
source: However, Cas9 activity on RNA is PAM-independent and may mitigate the effects of PAM-escape mutants that would evade DNA-level interference (Deveau et al., 2008), thus acting as an additional line of defense.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about biological function.

claim: SauCas9 cleavage efficiency is inversely related to structural complexity of the RNA target.
source: In conjunction with in vitro cleavage data of partially structured RNAs, we suggest that SauCas9 cleavage efficiency is inversely related to structural complexity of the RNA target.
evidence: This is inferred from the structured RNA experiments and MS2 screen data.

claim: Experimental knowledge about RNA structure, such as SHAPE-seq data, would simplify target identification for viral targeting and repression experiments.
source: As an alternative to the current approach of screening multiple sgRNAs for activity, experimental knowledge about RNA structure, such as SHAPE-seq data (Loughrey et al., 2014), would simplify target identification for viral targeting and repression experiments.
evidence: This is a proposed application based on the accessibility findings.

claim: SauCas9 could repress gene expression in E. coli.
source: SauCas9 holds promise for a range of RNA targeting applications. We showed that SauCas9 could repress gene expression in E. coli.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the GFP repression experiments.

claim: Repression of the reporter occurs in the absence of the PAM and is specific for targeting of the coding strand.
source: Repression of the reporter occurs in the absence of the PAM and is specific for targeting of the coding strand.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cas13 exhibits robust trans cleavage of RNAs.
source: 'Activated' Cas13 exhibits robust trans cleavage of RNAs(Abudayyeh et al., 2016; East-Seletsky et al., 2016; Smargon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on Cas13.

claim: RNA-cleavage by SauCas9 is single-turnover and kinetically less robust than that of Cas13.
source: While RNA-cleavage by SauCas9 is single-turnover and kinetically less robust than that of Cas13, Cas9 does not cleave RNAs indiscriminately and lends itself to targeting of specific transcripts.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the data presented and prior work on Cas13.

claim: Cas9 does not cleave RNAs indiscriminately and lends itself to targeting of specific transcripts.
source: While RNA-cleavage by SauCas9 is single-turnover and kinetically less robust than that of Cas13, Cas9 does not cleave RNAs indiscriminately and lends itself to targeting of specific transcripts.
evidence: This is inferred from the specificity data and comparison to Cas13.

claim: A programmable Cas9 capable of repressing genes on the RNA level has potential advantages over CRISPRi DNA-based techniques.
source: A programmable Cas9 capable of repressing genes on the RNA level has potential advantages over CRISPRi DNA-based techniques (Qi et al., 2013; Gilbert et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a proposed advantage discussed in the context of applications.

claim: Isoform-specific targeting of different transcripts originating from the same transcription start site or resulting from alternative splicing events might be possible with SauCas9.
source: For example, isoform-specific targeting of different transcripts originating from the same transcription start site or resulting from alternative splicing events might be possible.
evidence: This is a speculative application proposed based on RNA-level targeting.

claim: SauCas9 may have utility as a platform for directing other effector proteins to specific RNA molecules.
source: More broadly, due to its intrinsic ssRNA-binding activity, SauCas9 may have utility as a platform for directing other effector proteins to specific RNA molecules, such as proteins or domains that up-regulate translation or RNA base-modifying enzymes for site-specific epigenetic modification of RNAs.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal for future applications.
